responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character26_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll answer as Character26_F:

When I think about "fairness," for me it always came down to everyone having a shot, you know? Like, not everyone starts out with the same stuff in life—some people got handed more, some of us had to work for everything. Fairness isn’t about everyone getting the same thing, but about folks having a real chance to make something for themselves. I’ve seen enough of people getting pushed aside or judged before anyone knows their story. I think I always wanted things to be more level, so people like me—working class, or from families who didn’t have much—could actually get somewhere if we worked hard.

A "sense of belonging" is personal to me. Growing up, I always kind of felt like I was on the outside a bit. When you’re from a lower-income family, you notice it—at school, at work, even just walking into some places. Finding my people, where I didn’t have to pretend or explain myself, that’s what belonging felt like. I always thought everyone deserves that—to feel like they actually matter somewhere, not just tolerated.

As for "community," that’s the heart of it. Where I come from, your neighbors matter. People look out for each other because, sometimes, that’s all you got. Whether it’s helping someone out who lost their job, or just sharing a meal, it’s the small stuff that makes a community. But I’ve also seen how quick things can get divided—by race, money, whatever. I always felt it’s important to remember we’re all just trying to get by, and we’re better off if we stick together and help each other out.

Honestly, a lot of this comes from growing up in a place where things weren’t always easy, and from seeing how people judge or support you based on where you’re from or what you look like. That sticks with you and shapes how you see what’s fair, and what real community should be.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character26_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Honestly, if I’m sitting in the community garden just watching everyone, I feel a mix of things. Part of me likes it—seeing people from all different places, living their lives, sometimes bringing in their own food or ways of doing things. It kind of reminds me that the world’s bigger than just our little patch. I don’t mind different backgrounds—race, religion, even if someone’s got a different way of living. I grew up around people who were struggling for different reasons, so I try not to judge.

But to be real, sometimes it’s awkward, especially when you don’t know what to say, or you’re worried about saying the wrong thing. Or sometimes, you can feel like an outsider in your own neighborhood—like if there’s a big group speaking a language you don’t understand, or celebrating something you’re not part of. It’s not a bad thing, just feels weird, like maybe you don’t belong as much as you used to.

Most of the time, I’d rather just be friendly and mind my business. I’ll say hi, or help someone out if they need it, but I like when everyone respects each other’s space too. I do think it’s important to have a little effort from both sides—like, if someone’s new here, it helps if they try to learn how things work around here, but we should also try to make them feel welcome, you know? I don’t want anyone to feel shut out. I know what that’s like.

At the end of the day, I think it’s good to have different kinds of people around. It keeps things interesting, and you never know when you’ll need help or learn something new. But I also think it’s okay to admit it’s not always easy, and sometimes we gotta work at understanding each other.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah, I’ll talk about it. That’s real life, you know? In my neighborhood growing up, we had all kinds—people dealing with drinking, drugs, living together without being married, folks from other countries, even different religions. It wasn’t some postcard-perfect place. Everybody’s got their own stuff, and sometimes it shows.

I think what makes people comfortable is just being treated like a person. You don’t gotta go out of your way pretending nothing’s different, but you shouldn’t make folks feel small either. A simple hello, not staring, not gossiping about someone’s problems—stuff like that goes a long way. If someone’s got struggles, like addiction or sickness, I try to remember it could be me or someone I care about. I know sometimes it gets messy, or it’s hard to know what to say, but ignoring folks or acting like they’re dangerous just makes it worse.

For people from different backgrounds or lifestyles, communication is huge. Sometimes people judge because they don’t know what’s going on, or they’re scared of something new. I’ve seen arguments start just because someone thinks they’re being left out, or doesn’t understand a custom or language. A bit more talking—like sharing what’s important to you, or asking questions without being rude—can clear up a lot.

Tolerance is needed most when things rub up against what you’re used to. I’ve had neighbors who’d get mad about loud music during someone’s holiday, or not understand why two men living together are just a couple, not “roommates.” I think you gotta step back and remember everyone’s got their own way. You don’t have to agree or join in, but you should give people room to live.

I’m willing to talk about all this because I’ve seen what happens when people shut each other out—neighborhood gets cold, problems get worse, and nobody wins. I don’t want that. It’s not always easy, and sometimes you get uncomfortable, but a bit of respect and trying to understand goes a long way. We’re all here trying to make a life, even if it looks different. If we don’t talk and try to get along, the whole idea of community just falls apart.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character26_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough one. I’ll be honest—when jobs are tight, it’s something people around here talk about a lot. For me, fairness means looking out for the folks who’ve been here, who’ve paid in and built up the community, but also not forgetting that everyone’s just trying to survive.

If I had to choose, I think local residents should get first shot at jobs, especially the ones that keep a roof over your head and feed your family. It’s not about hating anyone from somewhere else—it’s just that when you see people you grew up with struggling, or hear about someone’s dad losing work and falling behind, you feel it. That’s why I think it’s fair to have some priority for locals, maybe for certain kinds of jobs or in hard times.

But I don’t think that means shutting the door completely on migrant workers. A lot of the time, they’re doing jobs nobody else wants, or filling gaps where there’s just not enough people. Plus, they’re often working just as hard, trying to send money home, and I respect that. Maybe there could be more support for training local people to do those jobs if they want them, or making sure wages and conditions are fair for everyone, so it’s not just a race to the bottom.

I guess I’d want a system where it’s clear who gets priority and why, but also one where people from outside aren’t treated like dirt. Maybe set up programs that help locals who’ve lost work first, but still let migrant workers fill spots if there’s a real need. We can’t blame people for coming here if their own situation is worse—you’d do the same if you had to.

It’s about balance. Make sure nobody’s being used or pushed aside, and try to keep things fair for the folks who’ve stuck with the community. But don’t forget that everyone’s just trying to make a living. That’s how I look at it.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character26_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Alright, looking at the big picture, I get why people feel so many different ways about immigration. It’s everywhere in the news and you see it in real life too. Some of those points make sense, some need more looking at.

First off, the idea that immigrants fill vital roles—I believe that. Where I’ve lived, a lot of jobs, especially hard labor or stuff in restaurants and cleaning, are done by people who came from somewhere else. Sometimes, locals won’t take those jobs, or there just aren’t enough hands. So yeah, immigrants do help out in lots of ways.

The talk about cultural diversity—making places more lively or interesting—I see that too. It’s nice to have new food, new festivals, and hear different languages sometimes. It can make the country feel less stuck in its ways. But it can also be tough for people who feel like things are changing too fast or don’t see themselves in their own area anymore.

Security concerns, though—I think people get worked up over this a lot. You hear about crime or terrorism, and some folks want to blame outsiders first. I think that needs real evidence, not just rumors or scary stories on TV. Most immigrants I’ve met are here to work and live quietly. Sure, you gotta check people out and make sure everyone’s safe, but blaming all problems on immigrants isn’t fair. That needs facts, not just feelings.

The humanitarian side—helping refugees and people from poor places—that’s important. I know what it’s like to struggle, and I wouldn’t wish that on anyone. If the country’s got the space and resources, I think we should help, but it needs to be managed so it doesn’t overwhelm what’s already stretched thin.

The fear about jobs and wages—that’s real for working class people. When you’re barely making ends meet and someone new comes in willing to do the job for less, it makes you nervous. Sometimes companies use immigrants to drive down pay or avoid unions. That’s not the immigrants’ fault, it’s the system, but it still hurts locals. I think that concern is reasonable, and government should make sure jobs pay enough, and that everyone has a chance.

So, some worries are reasonable—like jobs, or making sure things don’t change too fast for folks who’ve been here. Other concerns, like crime and terrorism, need real proof, and shouldn’t just be blamed on people coming in. I think more honest talk and better facts would help. Too much of this gets decided by fear or by people yelling on the internet, not by what’s actually happening. We need real stories and numbers, not just opinions.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character26_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I had to pick, I wouldn’t go for complete openness—just letting anyone in all the time feels risky when resources are tight and people here are already struggling. I don’t think shutting the door completely is right either; that’s too harsh and ignores that some people really need help, or that we actually need workers for some jobs.

I guess what makes sense to me is a mix: mainly admitting people based on job demand, but with some kind of numerical limits so things don’t get out of hand. Like, if there’s a real shortage—healthcare, farming, building—then let folks in for those jobs, but don’t let companies use it just to pay people less or skip over locals who want work. There should be rules so it doesn’t hurt the folks already here.

I’d also want to keep some room for refugees and people who are in real danger, but not so many that the system breaks and nobody gets good support. So, a set number for humanitarian reasons makes sense to me—help those who truly need it, but make sure it’s something the country can handle.

It’s important to check in every year or two: is the policy working, are locals still finding jobs, is the community holding together, are people getting along? If things start to go wrong, you slow down or tighten up. If it’s working and there’s more need, maybe you let a few more in.

So, I guess I’m for a balanced approach; one that’s flexible, uses real numbers about jobs and resources, and keeps the door open for those who really need safety. Fairness means not forgetting the people here who built this place, but also not blocking out people who just want a better life. Social integration takes time, but it works better when people feel the rules are fair and everyone gets a fair shot—including locals and newcomers.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character26_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character26_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Yeah, stepping into Character26_F’s shoes like this, I definitely saw things in a more personal way. It reminded me how much your background—how you grew up, what you struggled with—shapes the way you see what’s “fair.” For Character26_F, everything always came back to the real, day-to-day worries: having enough, feeling respected, not being ignored in your own home. When resources are short and you’re just trying to get by, policies don’t feel abstract—they feel like they hit you directly.

What stood out was how Character26_F wanted balance, not extremes. She wasn’t against immigrants, but she needed to know her community and people like her wouldn’t get left behind. That need for fairness wasn’t about shutting people out; it was about making sure the people who already feel invisible didn’t get pushed further to the margins. It’s easy to forget those feelings if you haven’t lived them, and this made me appreciate how important it is for policy to be grounded in ordinary people’s realities.

It also made me notice how easy it is for fear or change to make people uncomfortable—not because they’re closed-minded, but because they feel vulnerable. Talking as her, I realized how much she valued small gestures of respect and simple, honest communication. That’s not something statistics or headlines ever show.

For my own views, it made me think more about finding practical ways to balance compassion for newcomers with real support for locals. I see now how policies need to be flexible, responsive, and actually pay attention to what’s happening on the ground. It also reminded me that behind every opinion, there’s a whole history and set of experiences—like Character26_F’s—that deserve respect and understanding.
